subject: Agriculture
title: The Nile Basin Dispute
description: A quick win: understand The Nile Basin Dispute.

hook.text: Eleven countries share the Nile. Egypt uses most of the water—and Ethiopia is building a giant dam upstream.

buildup.text: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam will generate power for 60 million Ethiopians currently without electricity.

discovery.text: Egypt fears the dam will reduce its Nile flow. 95% of Egypt's water comes from the Nile.

twist.text: A 1959 treaty gave Egypt and Sudan nearly all Nile water. Ethiopia wasn't included and doesn't accept it.

climax.text: Negotiations have stalled for years. Control of the Nile could become Africa's most dangerous water conflict.

punchline.text: One river, eleven nations, zero agreement.

quiz.question: Why does Egypt oppose Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam?
options: Egypt depends on the Nile for 95% of its water and fears reduced flow

details.summary: The Nile Basin dispute is an ongoing conflict among 11 countries over the rights to use the Nile's water, primarily between Egypt, Sudan, and Ethiopia. This topic covers the colonial-era treaties, Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam, and the diplomacy surrounding shared water.
details.whyItMatters: The Nile supports over 250 million people, and Ethiopia's filling of its massive dam threatens Egypt's historical water share. Failure to reach agreement risks conflict in one of the world's most water-stressed regions.
takeaways: A 1959 treaty allocated virtually all Nile water to Egypt and Sudan, excluding upstream nations
Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam can store over 70 billion cubic meters of water
Negotiations have continued for over a decade without a binding agreement

faq.question: What is the core of the Nile Basin water dispute?
faq.answer: Egypt claims historical rights to most Nile water based on colonial-era treaties that excluded upstream nations. Ethiopia and other upstream countries argue they deserve a fair share to irrigate farms and generate hydroelectric power for their own development.

faq.question: Why is Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam controversial?
faq.answer: The dam on the Blue Nile—which provides 80% of Nile flow—could significantly reduce downstream flow to Egypt and Sudan during its filling phase. Egypt fears losing water essential for its agriculture, while Ethiopia sees the dam as vital for development.
